speaker: Doctor
text:
I notice you have yellowing of your skin and eyes, which suggests jaundice; have you been experiencing any abdominal pain, fever, or recent changes in your stool or urine color? To better understand the cause, I need to review your recent blood work.

REQUEST TEST: Liver Function Panel (ALT, AST, ALP, Bilirubin, Albumin, PT/INR)
REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
REQUEST TEST: Viral Hepatitis Serology (A, B, C)

How long have you noticed these symptoms, and do you have a history of alcohol use or medication intake?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Liver Function Panel: ALT 650 IU/L (elevated), AST 600 IU/L (elevated), Bilirubin 25 mg/dL (elevated), INR 1.5 (elevated), TP_Activity < 40% (reduced); Complete Blood Count: Hemoglobin 16.3 g/dL, Hematocrit 47%, Leukocyte Count 9,750/mm3, Neutrophils 58%, Bands 2%, Eosinophils 1%, Basophils 0%, Lymphocytes 24%, Monocytes 2%, Platelet Count 365,000/mm3; Viral Hepatitis Serology: Not Provided in available data.

speaker: Patient
text: 20-year-old male. The patient was previously healthy and has been brought to the emergency department due to agitation over the past 24 hours. Family members have noticed a yellowish coloring of his skin and eyes over the past week. The patient has a history of occasional cocaine and ecstasy use, and drinks alcohol socially on weekends. The patient also admits to high-risk sexual behaviors without using appropriate protection.

speaker: Patient
text: protection. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Acute appendicitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: I must clarify that the symptoms of yellow skin and eyes (jaundice) along with abnormal labs point to a liver issue, not appendicitis. To confirm the cause, please tell me: have you been consuming alcohol regularly or taking any new medications recently?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Social history: Occasional use of cocaine and ecstasy. Social alcohol consumption (about 20 g on weekends).

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your recent recreational drug use, could you specify if there were any episodes of overdose or if you experienced vomiting and abdominal pain around the time you took these substances? Also, have you noticed any dark urine or pale stools recently?

speaker: Patient
text: The patient shows signs of psychomotor agitation and confusion. No other symptoms provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Cocaine-Induced Hepatotoxicity with Acute Liver Failure. The combination of recent cocaine use, jaundice, agitation, and the exclusion of viral hepatitis or alcohol-induced disease strongly suggests a toxic metabolic injury from the drug overdose.
